patch.value: Ordering recorded as blocks is invisible to actionability: the same prerequisite schedules differently depending on which endpoint wrote it

The write path accepts an ordering constraint in two directions and only one of them reaches the scheduler.

collectBlockedByIds in src/core/item/actionability.ts resolves blockers from exactly two sources: the legacy scalar blocked_by field, and dependency rows whose kind equals the single literal BLOCKED_BY_DEPENDENCY_KIND declared at line 17. Its own docstring at line 31 states it is "the single source of truth for what must close before this item can proceed, shared by pm next readiness classification and the close-time auto-unblock sweep". The reverse spelling of the same relation, kind blocks, is an accepted member of the fifteen-spelling dependency vocabulary, is stored verbatim, and is honoured by the graph engine — yet it is invisible to every consumer of that single source of truth.

Proved in an isolated sandbox with two fresh items. Writing the constraint from the blocker side, B --dep id=A,kind=blocks, makes pm graph predecessors A return B and pm graph successors B return A, so the graph engine agrees that B precedes A. In the same workspace pm next reports A as ready with blocked count zero. Writing the identical constraint from the dependent side, C --dep id=D,kind=blocked_by, correctly reports C blocked by D. The asymmetry is silent in both directions: the blocked_by write leaves no mirror row on D, so reverse resolution exists for blocked_by alone.

Live corpus impact measured over every tracked item file: 219 blocks rows exist. Five active items are gated by a blocks source that is still open, and in all five the recorded gate is absent from the blocker set that pm next reports. pm-p1g43q is classified fully ready today while pm-07pt16, still open, declares blocks against it. The remaining four are latent rather than harmless: pm-3oqjnc reports blockers pm-lvyd only and omits pm-2vs1za, pm-li2fj5 omits pm-8bgeye, pm-qd6gvf omits pm-8bgeye, pm-pfqi omits pm-q7qojt. Each becomes wrongly ready the moment its unrelated blocked_by blocker closes, and nothing will flag it.

The multi-agent consequence is the reason this matters beyond hygiene. Two agents on two branches can record the same real prerequisite from opposite ends. The field-aware merge preserves both rows without conflict, exactly as designed, and the merged workspace then schedules the work differently depending on which endpoint happened to author the edge. Correctness of the queue becomes a function of authoring style rather than of the recorded constraint.

This is a conformance gap, not a missing feature. The closed ADR pm-9x6k defines ready as an active leaf with no open blocked_by, so the single-direction model was chosen deliberately; the write path then grew to accept the reverse spelling without canonicalizing it, which is the lexicon problem pm-4020c5 owns. pm-uxkf closed by unifying next, context and list-blocked onto one edge-aware definition, so all three surfaces now inherit the same blind spot from one place — which is also why one fix repairs all three. The downstream unblocks list built from the same reverse map is blind for the same reason.

Scope is the resolution rule and its canonicalization, not new vocabulary. Either the write path canonicalizes blocks into a blocked_by row on the referenced item, the way depends_on already canonicalizes, or blocker resolution reads the reverse direction of ordering kinds from the graph registry that already models it. Whichever is chosen, the 219 existing rows need a stated disposition and a check that keeps the two directions from diverging again.

A prerequisite recorded as blocks on the blocker produces the same readiness classification as the mirrored blocked_by row, proved by a paired test over both spellings; The disposition of the 219 existing blocks rows is recorded and applied, either by canonicalizing them on write or by resolving the reverse direction at read time; The blocker set pm next reports for the five currently affected items names the blocks gate, and pm-p1g43q is no longer classified ready while pm-07pt16 is open; The downstream unblocks projection resolves the same reverse direction as blocker resolution, with a test that fails if only one of the two is fixed; A check fails when an ordering kind accepted by the write path is not reachable by blocker resolution, so a new spelling cannot reintroduce the divergence

value.text:
Reproducer, verified 2026-07-28 in an isolated sandbox with PM_PATH and PM_GLOBAL_PATH outside the repo.

Two fresh Tasks, A and B. One mutation: pm update B --dep id=A,kind=blocks.

Graph engine agrees the ordering exists: pm graph predecessors A returns count 1 ids [B]; pm graph successors B returns count 1 ids [A]; pm graph successors A and predecessors B are both empty.

Scheduler disagrees: pm next reports recommended B, ready [A], blocked [], summary blocked 0. A is offered as work while its recorded predecessor is open.

Mirrored control in the same workspace: pm update C --dep id=D,kind=blocked_by yields pm next blocked [(C, blockers [D])], correct. pm get D shows dependencies [] — the blocked_by write stores no mirror row, so reverse resolution is implemented for blocked_by only and the two spellings are not interchangeable.

Live census method, over every tracked item .toon file rather than a list projection: parse the dependencies[N]{id,kind,...} header then consume indented CSV rows until the first non-indented line. Declared rows total 8,012 with kinds related 4,930, implements 2,014, parent 275, discovered_from 220, blocks 219, verifies 139, blocked_by 127, supersedes 55, related_to 16, child 15, incident_from 2. Do not reconcile these against pm graph audit profile.edges_by_kind, which reports the registry graph after read-side canonicalization and after folding the parent scalar into edges; the two series are not comparable and never have been.

Note the ratio the census exposes: 219 blocks rows against 127 declared blocked_by rows. The spelling the scheduler cannot see is the more common of the two.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Third consequence of the asymmetry, discovered by accident while wiring this item and worth keeping because it closes off the obvious workaround.

The natural mitigation an agent would reach for is to record the constraint from both ends, so that the graph engine and the scheduler each see the spelling they understand. That does not work. Adding blocks rows on pm-4020c5 against this item and against pm-1w6scp, while the mirrored blocked_by rows already existed on the two dependents, immediately produced two regressions on a previously clean tracker: pm graph audit went from 11 findings to 12 with a new duplicate_edge finding, and pm validate gained a new warning class, validate_lifecycle_dependency_cycles with count 1. Both rows named the same direction — pm-4020c5 precedes the dependent — so the pair is not reciprocal and asserts no contradiction, yet the lifecycle checker canonicalizes the reverse spelling and then sees an edge in each direction between the same two nodes.

The rows were reverted and both signals returned to baseline, 11 findings and six warning classes, confirming the pair was the sole cause.

So the three spellings of one prerequisite each fail differently: blocked_by alone is correct but invisible to the graph consumers that read the other direction, blocks alone is invisible to the scheduler, and both together are a validation error. There is no way for an author to express an ordering constraint that every consumer reads correctly, which is why the fix has to be canonicalization at the write path rather than guidance about which spelling to prefer.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Companion finding on the write and lifecycle side, filed 2026-07-31 as pm-xm0id4. Together the two items describe a trap with no correct move for an author.

This item proves the read-side asymmetry: a prerequisite recorded as blocks is honoured by the graph engine and invisible to collectBlockedByIds, so it never reaches readiness classification. The new finding proves the lifecycle-side asymmetry on the other spelling: clearClosedBlockerSignals at src/cli/commands/close.ts:626 deletes every blocked_by row when the item holding it closes, so the spelling that IS visible to the scheduler does not survive into history.

The corpus shows both halves at once. blocked_by is held by 91 of 318 open items and by exactly 1 of 1,900 closed items. blocks is held by 4 open items and 189 closed ones. So the two spellings partition the corpus almost perfectly by lifecycle state, and neither one is both actionable while open and durable after close. An author who picks blocked_by gets scheduling and no history; an author who picks blocks gets history and no scheduling.

That sharpens this item's multi-agent argument. Two agents recording the same real prerequisite from opposite ends do not merely schedule differently, as this item establishes - they also leave records with different lifetimes. After both items close, the branch that wrote blocks still has the edge and the branch that wrote blocked_by does not, so the field-aware merge preserves an asymmetry that was never authored as one.

Whichever disposition this item chooses for the 219 blocks rows should be decided jointly with pm-xm0id4's retention semantics, because canonicalizing blocks into blocked_by rows - one of the two options this item names - would move 189 surviving historical edges into the field that the close path clears, and the next close of any of those items would delete them.

value.text: The declared 241 ceiling fired against a maintenance agent on 2026-08-08 and blocked a release dry run at 243. Both new rows were mine, added minutes earlier while enriching this session's lineage, and both were wrong in exactly the way this item describes: the intended relation was that a general defect was discovered from two specific ones, which the graph already carried as discovered_from, and blocks was reached for because it is the reflex spelling for any ordering intuition. Neither edge expressed a prerequisite and neither would have scheduled anything. This is useful evidence for the item's thesis rather than for its count. The population does not grow because anyone decides ordering should be recorded as blocks; it grows because blocks is the default reach when a relation feels directional, and nothing at write time asks whether a prerequisite is actually being asserted or from which endpoint. Rows removed by exact id and kind selector, restoring 241; the ratchet then passed at 26 enforced bounds.
